passages.title: Seven oaths and the soul's two destinies
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

Allah takes seven oaths — by the sun, the moon, the day, the night, the sky, the earth, and finally the human soul — and then swears to a single truth: that a person's whole destiny turns on what he does with his own soul. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that Allah swears "by the objects and phenomena mentioned in verses [1–7]," and then, coming to ayat 9–10, states plainly: "This is the subject of the seven oaths."

Ayah 8 belongs with ayah 7 rather than standing alone. Maʿārif notes that the sentence "then with the knowledge of right and wrong inspired it" is "linked with the seventh oath" — the soul Allah made well is the same soul Allah then equipped to tell good from bad.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also draws out why Allah swears by these things at all: it "gives these creations an added significance and draws man's attention to them. Man ought to reflect on these phenomena and try to appreciate their value and the purpose of their creation."

---

## The shape of the oath: from the cosmos inward

Read the seven in the order they are given and notice the movement. Sun, moon, day, night — the rhythm you live inside. Then sky and earth — the two halves of the world. Then, last, *your own self*.

That last member of the list is where the whole passage is heading. Maʿārif's instruction — reflect on these things, appreciate their value and the purpose of their creation — lands hardest when the thing to be reflected on is you.

---

## Opening the words

**Ayah 1 — "By the sun and its brightness."** The Arabic is *wa'sh-shamsi wa ḍuḥāhā*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that although the phrase "his broad light" is joined to "by the sun" by the connector *and*, the context shows it is really describing the sun: the sense is "I swear by the sun when it is in the time of forenoon."

**Ḍuḥā**, Maʿārif says, is that part of the day "when the sun rises [early in the morning] and goes up slightly higher [on the sky], and its light spreads on the earth." And then a lovely observation: "Man observes it to be near to himself and observes it fully on account of lack of heat." It is the sun at the hour you can actually look at it.

Ibn Kathir records the early readings: Mujahid said *ḍuḥāhā* means "by its light"; Qatadah said it means "the whole day." Ibn Jarir judged: "The correct view is what has been said, 'Allah swears by the sun and its daytime, because the clear light of the sun is daytime.'"

**Ayah 2 — "and the moon as it follows it."** Mujahid said the moon "follows it (the sun)." Ibn ʿAbbas, as reported by al-ʿAwfi, said "It follows the day." Qatadah related it to the night of the *hilāl*, the new crescent: "When the sun goes down, the Hilal is visible." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possibilities: that "the moon following the sun is seen clearly during the middle of the lunar months when the full moon rises to dominate the sky with its radiance after sunset"; or that "just as the sun is seen in full in broad light, so does the moon, following the sun, become full."

**Ayah 3 — "and the day as it unveils it."** *Jallāhā* — Mujahid said, "When it illuminates," and compared it to *wa'n-nahāri idhā tajallā*, "By the day as it Tajalla" (92:2).

Maʿārif raises a grammatical point worth pausing on. The attached pronoun *hā* ("its") has no clearly stated antecedent. It may refer to the earth or the world even though neither noun precedes it — Arabic does this readily with things everyone is familiar with, referring to them by a pronoun alone and leaving the listener to understand by implication; the Qurʼān has many examples. On that reading the ayah means "by the day and by the world or the earth which the day has brightened up" — in other words, "by the day when it is fully bright."

But Maʿārif considers a second possibility "more pertinent to the context": that *hā* refers to the sun, so it signifies "by the day when it brightens up the sun." Maʿārif calls this "a metaphorical relationship," since the sun is usually understood to be the cause of the day, yet here the day is said to brighten the sun. It captures something real: "when the sun is seen brightened up because the day is out."

**Ayah 4 — "and the night as it conceals it."** Ibn Kathir's authorities say *yaghshāhā* means when the night covers the sun — "which takes place when sun disappears and the horizons become dark." Maʿārif: "when it [the night] sets in, the brightness of the sun is concealed [and only darkness prevails]."

**Ayat 5–6 — "And by heaven and the One Who built it, and the earth and the One Who spread it."** Here the commentators genuinely differ over one small word, *mā*.

- Taken as *maṣdariyyah* (an infinitival particle, which turns the verb into a verbal noun), the meaning is "by the sky and its make" and "by the earth and its expanse." Ibn Kathir attributes the first to Qatadah: "By the heaven and its construction." Maʿārif says the context most clearly suggests this reading, compares it to the usage in 36:27 ("…how my Lord has forgiven me"), and notes that Qatadah and others reported this interpretation and that *Kashshāf*, Baiḍāwī and Qurṭubī preferred it.
- Taken as *mawṣūlah* (a relative pronoun in the sense of *man*, "the One Who"), the meaning is "by the heaven and its Constructor" and "by the earth and the One who spreads it." Ibn Kathir attributes this to Mujahid; Maʿārif notes that some commentators take *mā* this way and refer it to Allah, and that this is the construction Maulana Thanawi adopted — which is why the translation before you reads "the One Who built it."

Ibn Kathir's verdict is irenic: "Both views are interrelated, and construction means raising." He cites *wa's-samāʼa banaynāhā bi-aydin* — "With Hands did We construct the heaven" (51:47) — which he glosses as *meaning, with strength* — along with 51:47–48, "Verily, We are able to extend the vastness of space thereof. And We have spread out the earth: how excellent a spreader are We!"

Maʿārif draws out the upshot: in these two ayat "attention has been focused on the great Designer and Architect of the sky and earth [that is, the universe], and on the perfection and complete freedom from flaw or defect in the design and creation of the universe." Maʿārif also observes, with due caution, that up to this point all the oaths had been by created objects and phenomena, while on the second reading an oath is here taken by Allah — "And Allah knows best!"

On *ṭaḥāhā* (ayah 6), Ibn Kathir reports a broad agreement of the early scholars — Mujahid, Qatadah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, as-Suddī, ath-Thawrī, Abū Ṣāliḥ and Ibn Zayd — that it means *He spread it out*. Ibn ʿAbbas is reported through al-ʿAwfi as saying it means "what He created in it," and through ʿAli bin Abi Ṭalḥah as saying "He proportioned it." Maʿārif adds simply that "the word *tahwun* means 'to spread'."

---

## Ayah 7: the soul, made well

*Wa nafsin wa mā sawwāhā* — "And by the soul and the One Who fashioned it."

Maʿārif notes the same two readings of *mā* here: as an infinitival particle it signifies "by the human soul and its perfection"; taken in the sense of *man* it signifies "by the soul and the One who proportioned it." And Maʿārif glosses the key word: *taswiyah* "means, to proportion, balance, perfect."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is the heart of it: Allah "created it sound and well-proportioned upon the correct nature (Al-Fiṭrah)," and he cites, "Allah's Fiṭrah with which He has created mankind. No change let there be in the Khalqillah [the creation of Allah]" (30:30).

Two hadith come in here. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Every child that is born, is born upon the Fiṭrah, but his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Zoroastrian. This is just as the animal is born, complete with all of its parts. Do you notice any mutilation in it?" — recorded, Ibn Kathir says, by both Al-Bukhari and Muslim from Abu Hurayrah. And in Sahih Muslim, narrated from ʿIyāḍ bin Ḥimār al-Mujāshiʿī, the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah the Mighty and Majestic says, "Verily I created My servants Ḥunafāʼ (as monotheists), but then the devils came to them and distracted them from their religion."

So the soul comes from Allah sound and rightly aligned, like a newborn animal with every part intact. Whatever crookedness it later carries came in from somewhere else.

---

## Ayah 8: shown both roads

*Fa-alhamahā fujūrahā wa taqwāhā* — "then with the knowledge of right and wrong inspired it!" Ibn Kathir renders it, "Then He showed it its Fujur and its Taqwa."

Maʿārif explains the vocabulary as far as it goes: **ilhām** "denotes 'to cast into the heart'," and **fujūr** "denotes 'open transgression'." Of the third word it says only this — "The meaning of *taqwa* is well-known" — and leaves it there, so we will too.

Ibn Kathir: "He showed him to his transgression and his Taqwa. This means that He clarified that for it and He guided it to what has been ordained for him." Ibn ʿAbbas said, "He explained the good and the evil to it (the soul)" — and Mujahid, Qatadah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and ath-Thawrī all said the same. Saʿid bin Jubayr: "He gave him inspiration (to see what was) good and evil." Ibn Zayd put it most strikingly: "He made its Fujūr and its Taqwā *inside* of it."

Note the order across the two ayat: first the soul is made well, then it is shown both roads. You were not left to guess.

### The question of qadar

Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Jarir, through Abul-Aswad ad-Dīlī, that ʿImrān bin Ḥuṣayn pressed him on whether what people do and strive for is preordained, or only written after the Message reaches them. Abul-Aswad answered that it is "something preordained upon them." ʿImrān then asked, "Is that an injustice?" — and Abul-Aswad, by his own account extremely frightened by the question, answered, "There is nothing except that He (Allah) created it and possesses it in His Hand. He is not asked about what He does, while they (His creation) will be asked."

ʿImrān then explained that he had only asked in order to relate that a man of Muzaynah or Juhaynah put the same question to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who replied, "Rather it is something preordained for them." The man said, "Then what is the point of our actions?" The Prophet ﷺ answered: "Whoever Allah created for one of the two positions (Paradise or Hell), He makes it easy for him (to attain)" — and he gave ayat 7 and 8 as the proof of that in the Book of Allah. Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad and Muslim both recorded this hadith.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing a hadith transmitted by Muslim on the authority of Sayyidnā ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn — in which the Prophet ﷺ was asked about divine destiny and recited this ayah in reply — draws out the other side of the same coin. This ayah allays the doubt about divine destiny, Maʿārif says, when its words are taken to mean that "Allah has equipped man with human soul which has the capacity to distinguish between good and bad, and right and wrong," that "in his make-up Allah has built in him a special ability to choose freely the righteous path or the sinful path," and that the soul "has been inspired with conscience to distinguish between right and wrong, and has also been granted the ability to do good as well as the ability to commit sin." Man, it concludes, "is not a creature of pure force or coercion. He has free will to choose his path of good or evil… The choice is his, for which he is rewarded or punished."

Both are affirmed here and neither is explained away: Allah's decree encompasses everything and He is not asked about what He does, and the choosing you do is genuinely yours and you will be asked about it. What the passage asks of you is not to solve that, but to *act* — and, as the next section shows, to beg Allah for help while acting.

---

## From the Sunnah: the duʿāʼ he ﷺ would stop to make

At-Tabarani recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "used to stop whenever he recited this Ayah" — ayat 7–8 — and then would say:

> "O Allah! Give my soul its good. You are its Guardian and Master, and the best to purify it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same practice from Sayyidnā Abu Hurairah and Ibn ʿAbbas: that whenever he ﷺ recited ayat 7–8 he would stop and recite this supplication aloud.

And Imam Ahmad recorded that Zayd bin Arqam said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "O Allah! Verily, I seek refuge with You from weakness, laziness, senility (of old age), cowardliness, stinginess and the torment of the grave. O Allah! Give my soul its good and purify it, for You are the best to purify it. You are its Guardian and Master. O Allah! Verily, I seek refuge with You from a heart that is not humble, a soul that is not satisfied, knowledge that does not benefit and a supplication that is not answered."

Zayd added, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to teach us these (words) and we now teach them to you." Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim also recorded this hadith.

That pause is itself a lesson. He ﷺ, to whom this revelation came, would not recite past ayah 8 without asking Allah for his own soul's good.

---

## Ayat 9–10: the two destinies

*Qad aflaḥa man zakkāhā — wa qad khāba man dassāhā.* "Successful indeed is the one who purifies their soul, and doomed is the one who corrupts it!" Maʿārif renders the pair: "success is really attained by him who purifies it, and failure is really suffered by him who pollutes it."

**Zakkā / tazkiyah.** Maʿārif: "the primitive meaning of *tazkiyah* is 'inner cleanliness', signifying 'he who obeyed Allah and purified his inner and outer selves'." Ibn Kathir: this "could mean that whoever purifies himself by obedience to Allah, then he will be successful," and he quotes Qatadah — "He cleanses it from the lowly and despicable characteristics" — noting that similar was reported from Mujahid, ʿIkrimah and Saʿid bin Jubayr.

**Dassā.** This is the word that repays study. Maʿārif traces it to the root *dass*, "which denotes 'to bury in the ground'," as it occurs elsewhere in the Qurʼān: *am yadussuhu fi't-turāb*, "…or put it away into the dust?" (16:59). Ibn Kathir gives the sense as "to conceal it. This means that he makes it dull, and he disregards it by neglecting to allow it to receive guidance. He treats it in this manner until he performs acts of disobedience and he abandons obedience of Allah." Maʿārif: "he who caused his soul to sink in the swamp of sins will be deprived."

Set the two verbs side by side. One man cleanses his soul of the lowly and despicable and obeys Allah with his inner and outer self. The other, in the image the root itself supplies, puts his out of sight — letting it go dull, declining to let guidance reach it, until that inner capacity to tell good from bad (ayah 8) has been buried under the habit of disobedience.

**A second reading.** Ibn Kathir notes it "also could mean that he is indeed successful whose soul Allah purifies, and he has failed whose soul Allah corrupts," reported from Ibn ʿAbbas through al-ʿAwfi and through ʿAli bin Abi Ṭalḥah. Maʿārif likewise mentions commentators who take the pronouns in *zakkā* and *dassā* as referring to Allah. Both readings stand, and together they match the duʿāʼ above exactly: strive to purify your soul, and ask the One who is "the best to purify it" to do it.

Maʿārif observes that this ayah "has divided the entire mankind into two groups: [1] successful; and [2] unsuccessful" — and that the sūrah then cites an example of the second group, showing how it rejected the message of Allah and how Allah consequently destroyed them. Such a group "will receive severe punishment in the Hereafter," though "sometimes… an installment of punishment is meted out to them in this world as in the case of Thamud," whose story the sūrah goes on to touch briefly.

---

## Living it

**Nothing here is out of reach.** The soul you were given was created "sound and well-proportioned upon the correct nature" (ayah 7) and then shown its transgression and its taqwā (ayah 8). You are not being asked to acquire something you lack; you are being asked not to bury what you already have.

**Purification is by obedience.** Qatadah's definition is concrete: cleansing the soul "from the lowly and despicable characteristics." Ibn Kathir frames it as purifying oneself *by obedience to Allah*; Maʿārif as obeying Allah and purifying "his inner and outer selves." Name a vice, work on it, and keep the obligations — that is *tazkiyah*.

**Beware of gradual burial.** Ibn Kathir describes the failure of ayah 10 as neglect: making the soul dull, disregarding it, declining to let it receive guidance — and continuing in that manner until disobedience is what one does and obedience to Allah is abandoned. It creeps.

**Make his duʿāʼ your own.** Do what he ﷺ did — stop at ayat 7–8 and ask: *Allāhumma āti nafsī taqwāhā, anta waliyyuhā wa mawlāhā, wa anta khayru man zakkāhā.* "O Allah! Give my soul its good. You are its Guardian and Master, and the best to purify it."

**One more sunnah from this sūrah.** Ibn Kathir opens his commentary under the heading "Recitation of Surah Ash-Shams wa Duhaha in the ʿIshāʼ Prayer," recalling the hadith of Jabir recorded in the Two Sahihs, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Muʿadh, "Why didn't you pray with (the recitation of) *Sabbiḥ isma rabbika'l-aʿlā* (87), *Wa'sh-shamsi wa ḍuḥāhā* (91), and *Wa'l-layli idhā yaghshā* (92)?"

passages.title: Thamud's defiance and total destruction
passages.tafsir:
# Thamūd's Defiance and Total Destruction (91:11–15)

**What this passage is about.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes ayat 9–10 — *success is really attained by him who purifies it, and failure is really suffered by him who pollutes it* — as "the subject of the seven oaths" that opened the sūrah. Having stated that principle, the sūrah stops arguing and simply points: *look at Thamūd.* These five ayat are a single compressed narrative — a nation's arrogance, one man's crime, a prophet's warning, the slaughter of a sign, and a punishment that fell on every last one of them.

**What holds them together.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the connection explicit: ayat 9–10 divide the entire mankind into two groups, the successful and the unsuccessful. What follows is an example of the second group — how it rejected the message of Allah and how Allah consequently destroyed them. Such a group, Maʿārif adds, will receive severe punishment in the Hereafter; sometimes, however, an *instalment* of that punishment is meted out in this world, as in the case of Thamūd. This is only a brief reference here; Maʿārif notes their story is recounted fully elsewhere in the Qur'ān (Sūrah al-Aʿrāf 7:73–79, and 11:61–68, 26:141–159, 27:45–53, 41:17–18, 54:23–32, 69:4–5).

---

## Ayah 11 — the root was transgression, not ignorance

*"Thamûd rejected ˹the truth˺ out of arrogance."*

The Arabic is **kadhdhabat Thamūdu bi-ṭaghwāhā** — they denied *by means of* their ṭaghwā. The translations render this key word differently: "out of arrogance," and in Ibn Kathīr's rendering, "through their transgression." Both are reaching for the same idea, and Ibn Kathīr spells it out: Allah informs us that Thamūd rejected their Messenger **because of the injustice and transgression they practiced**. This, he says, was said by Mujāhid, Qatādah and others.

Notice the direction of cause, because Ibn Kathīr is careful about it. The transgression comes first, and *therefore*, in his words, "this resulted in a rejection in their hearts for the guidance and conviction their Messenger came to them with." On this reading the wrongdoing was not the symptom of the disbelief; it was what produced it. A soul already practising injustice had nowhere to put a message that called it to account — which is precisely the soul ayah 10 described as buried and stifled.

## Ayah 12 — "the most wicked of them was roused"

*"when the most wicked of them was roused ˹to kill the she-camel˺."*

**ashqāhā** — "their most wicked." Ibn Kathīr explains it as the most wicked person of the tribe, and identifies him as **Qudār ibn Sālif**, the one who killed the she-camel, and the leader of the tribe of Thamūd. He is the one Allah refers to elsewhere: *"But they called their comrade and he took (a sword) and killed (her)"* (54:29).

Ibn Kathīr then adds something easy to miss. This was not a marginal figure. **"This man was mighty and respected among his people. He was of noble lineage and a leader who was obeyed."** Set that description beside the word the Qur'ān chooses for him — *ashqāhā*, their most wicked — and the two run in opposite directions. What his people counted as standing counted for nothing in the naming Allah gave him.

### From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathīr reports that Imām Aḥmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn Zamʿah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave a sermon in which he mentioned the she-camel and mentioned the man who killed her, and then recited *"When their most wicked went forth"* and said:

> "A strong and mighty man who was invincible among his tribe, like Abū Zamʿah, went forth to her."

Ibn Kathīr states that this ḥadīth was recorded by **al-Bukhārī in his Book of Tafsīr**, and **Muslim in his Book of the Description of the Hellfire**, and that **at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī** both recorded it in their *Sunans*, in their Books of Tafsīr.

The Prophet ﷺ is not describing a monster. He is describing a man of strength and standing whom no one in his own circle could restrain.

## Ayah 13 — a prophet's last warning

*"But the messenger of Allah warned them, '˹Do not disturb˺ Allah's she-camel and her drink!'"*

Ibn Kathīr notes that **"the Messenger of Allah"** here refers to **Ṣāliḥ**. The Arabic of his warning is extraordinarily terse — just two phrases, **nāqat Allāhi wa suqyāhā**, "the she-camel of Allah, and her drink" — which is why translations have to supply a verb ("Be cautious!", "Do not disturb"). Ibn Kathīr supplies the sense in exactly that way:

- **nāqat Allāh** — *"That is the she-camel of Allah!"* — meaning, in his gloss, *"beware of touching the she-camel of Allah with any harm."*
- **wa suqyāhā** — *"and its drink!"* — meaning, *"do not transgress against her in her drinking, for she has been allocated a day to drink and you have been allocated a day to drink, as is known to you."*

Two details deserve attention. First, the camel is attributed to Allah — *the she-camel of Allah* — an attribution of honour that placed her beyond harm. Ibn Kathīr says later in the same passage that she was the animal **Allah had brought out of the rock as a sign for them and a proof against them**. A miracle produced from solid stone stood grazing among them.

Second, the arrangement over water: a day for her, a day for them, "as is known to you." They had every other day. The whole conflict came down to one limit set by Allah on a resource they considered theirs.

## Ayah 14 — the sentence

*"Still they defied him and slaughtered her. So their Lord crushed them for their sin, levelling all."*

**fa-kadhdhabūhu fa-ʿaqarūhā** — "Then they denied him and they killed it." Ibn Kathīr explains: this "means they rejected what he came with. This resulted in them killing the she-camel that Allah had brought out of the rock as a sign for them and a proof against them." In his account, the denial and the blade are one sequence, not two separate events.

**fa-damdama ʿalayhim rabbuhum bi-dhanbihim.** Ibn Kathīr's gloss on *damdama* is short and heavy: **"He became angry with them and He annihilated them."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word further: *damdama* "refers to such tormenting scourge as is unleashed on a person or a nation again and again, until it destroys or crushes them completely." This is not a warning shot.

Note also **rabbuhum**, *their Lord*. Not "Allah destroyed them" but *their own Lord* — the one who sent them a messenger and brought a she-camel out of the rock as a sign for them. And **bi-dhanbihim**, *because of their sin*: the sentence is stated with its cause attached. Nothing arbitrary happened here.

### "Fasawwāhā" — and why *everyone* died

**fa-sawwāhā.** Ibn Kathīr: **"He made the punishment descend upon them all equally."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: *fa-sawwāhā* "signifies that the scourge overtook the entire nation, men, women, children, and young and old."

This raises the obvious question — one man drew the sword, so why did an entire nation fall? Ibn Kathīr answers it with a report from Qatādah:

> "It has reached us that the leader of tribe of Thamūd did not kill the she-camel until their youth, their elderly, their males and their females all pledged allegiance to him. So when the people cooperated in killing her, Allah destroyed them all with the same punishment due to their sin."

That is why ayah 11 opens by naming **Thamūd** — the whole people — and ayah 14 says **"they** denied him and **they** killed her," even though ayah 12 names a single man. The hand was one; on Qatādah's report the pledge behind it was universal. Qudār ibn Sālif was not acting alone; he was acting with the allegiance of young and old, male and female, already given.

## Ayah 15 — "And He feared not the consequences thereof"

*"He has no fear of consequences."*

**wa lā yakhāfu ʿuqbāhā.** Ibn Kathīr notes that this has **also been recited** as *fa-lā yakhāfu*, "So He feared not."

On the meaning, Ibn Kathīr reports **Ibn ʿAbbās**: *"Allah does not fear any consequences from anyone else."* He adds that **Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Bakr ibn ʿAbdullāh al-Muzanī and others all said the same.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out with a comparison that lands immediately. Divine torment that destroys a nation completely cannot be compared to the torment inflicted by the greatest king of this world, "because a tyrant king who destroys his people on a large scale, fears for his life, lest the survivors or the supporters of the people destroyed should revenge on him and rebel against him. Whoever destroys others is himself in danger of avenge. Those who attack others must necessarily bear the brunt of counter-attack except Allah."

So this closing ayah is a statement about absolute divine sovereignty. Every earthly power that kills does so with one eye on the aftermath: the retaliation, the survivors, the coalition that forms afterwards. Allah has no aftermath to manage. As Maʿārif puts it: when a people incur Divine punishment and are thus destroyed, Allah has no fear from anyone.

---

## Living it

**Small limits are the real test.** Thamūd were not asked to give up much — a day of water in two, "as is known to you." The boundaries that look trivial are often exactly where a soul discovers whether it will accept being commanded at all.

**Consent is participation.** Qatādah's report is uncomfortable by design: the sword waited for a pledge. Young and old, men and women gave it — and the punishment came down on every one of them equally. Where a wrong is authorised in our name, we do not get to point only at the hand that held the knife.

**Prestige proves nothing.** The man Ibn Kathīr describes as mighty, respected, noble in lineage and obeyed — the man the Prophet ﷺ described as strong and invincible among his tribe — is the man the Qur'ān calls *ashqāhā*, their most wicked. Allah's evaluation and the community's evaluation ran in opposite directions.

**And the counterweight.** Read against ayat 9–10, the passage is not only a threat. If a soul can be so thoroughly buried, it can also be purified — and Maʿārif notes that some of the commentators read the pronouns of *zakkā* and *dassā* as referring to Allah, signifying *"he is successful indeed whose soul Allah has purified."* Thamūd is what the other road looks like when it is walked to the end.
